title: Crossing a river or stream on foot
asks: how to cross a river safely
crossing a fast stream on foot
how do i ford a river

how to cross a river with a group

river is high and fast and we need to get across, how, over
answer: Moving water is dangerous. FEMA warns that six inches of moving water may be enough to knock you off your feet, and that flood water depth is hard to determine and may contain hidden, dangerous debris. At a flooded roadway: turn around.
Make a plan before crossing. First go to a high place for a good view of the river or stream, and look for a place to cross.
Cross streams where the water level is lowest.
Good places to cross: a level stretch where the river breaks into several channels (two or three narrow channels are usually easier to cross than a wide river), or a shallow bank or sandbar.

If possible, start from a point upstream of the bank or sandbar, so that the current will carry you to it if you lose your footing. Pick a course that leads downstream, so that you cross the current at about a 45-degree angle.

Avoid these places if possible: a ledge of rocks that crosses the river, which often indicates dangerous rapids or canyons; an estuary, which is normally wide, has strong currents and is subject to tides (go back upstream to an easier crossing site); and eddies, which can pull you under the surface.
To ford a swift, treacherous stream, find a strong pole about 3 inches in diameter and 7 to 8 feet long.

Grasp the pole and plant it firmly on the upstream side to break the current. Plant your feet firmly with each step. Move the pole forward a little downstream from its previous position, but still upstream.

With the next step, place your foot below the pole. Keep the pole well slanted, so that the force of the current keeps it against your shoulder. Cross so that you move across the downstream current at a 45-degree angle.

If other people are with you, all cross the stream together. Position the heaviest person on the downstream end of the pole and the lightest person on the upstream end. The upstream person breaks the current; if that person temporarily loses footing, the others can hold steady.
If you must swim a deep, swift river: swim with the current, not against it, and try to keep your body horizontal to the water. This reduces the danger of being pulled under.
In fast, shallow rapids: lie on your back, feet pointing downstream, finning your hands alongside your hips. Keep your feet up to avoid getting them caught by rocks.
In deep rapids: lie on your stomach, head downstream, angling toward the shore. Watch for obstacles, and be careful of backwater eddies and converging currents, which often contain dangerous swirls.
warnings: After a flood, avoid wading in floodwater: it can contain dangerous debris and be contaminated.

Cold water: sudden immersion triggers a cold-shock reflex, an instantaneous gasping for air. It can be deadly if your head is underwater, or if you have no flotation and cannot keep your head above the water.

The Army's 1-10-1 rule for accidental cold-water immersion: about 1 minute to get over the cold shock and resume breathing normally (most people die from drowning in this first minute); then about 10 minutes to get out of the cold water before the muscles fatigue; then about an hour before moderate to severe hypothermia sets in. The HHS ship's medical manual says the cold-shock reflex lasts for a few minutes.
If you use a flotation device, test it before trying to use it.

quotes.text: When you come across flooded roadways: Turn Around, Don’t Drown®. Six inches of moving water may be enough to knock you off your feet. As little as 12 inches of moving water may lift a small vehicle. Flood water depth is hard to determine and may contain hidden, dangerous debris.
After a flood, avoid wading in floodwater, which can contain dangerous debris and be contaminated.

Before crossing a river or stream, a good plan will need to be developed. The first step is to look for a high place from which to get a good view of the river or stream. From here, the isolated persons can look for a place to cross.
Cross-streams where the water level is lowest.
Good crossing locations include
A level stretch where it breaks into several channels. Two or three narrow channels are usually easier to cross than a wide river.
A shallow bank or sandbar. If possible, select a point upstream from the bank or sandbar so that the current will carry them to it if they lose their footing.
A course across the river that leads downstream so that isolated persons will cross the current at about a 45- degree angle.
The following areas possess potential hazards; avoid them if possible:
A ledge of rocks that crosses the river. This often indicates dangerous rapids or canyons.

An estuary of a river, because it is normally wide, has strong currents and is subject to tides. These tides can influence some rivers many miles from their mouths; personnel should go back upstream to an easier crossing site.
Eddies, which can produce a powerful backward pull downstream of the obstruction causing the eddy and pull personnel under the surface.

Converging currents occur where new watercourses enter the river or where water has been diverted around large obstacles such as small islands. To ford a swift, treacherous stream, apply the following steps:
Step 1. Find a strong pole about 3 inches in diameter and 7 to 8 feet long to help ford the stream.

Step 2. Grasp the pole and plant it firmly on the upstream side to break the current. Plant feet firmly with each step, and move the pole forward a little downstream from its previous position, but still upstream.

Step 3. With the next step, place foot below the pole. Keep the pole well slanted so that the force of the current keeps the pole against their shoulder. Cross the stream in such a manner that the downstream current is being crossed at a 45-degree angle

If there are other people with the isolated person, ensure that they all cross the stream together. Position the heaviest person on the downstream end of the pole and the lightest person on the upstream end

In using this method, the upstream person breaks the current, and those below can move with relative ease in the eddy formed by the upstream person. If the upstream person temporarily loses footing, the others can hold steady while the upstream person regains footing.

To swim across a deep, swift river, swim with the current; do no swim against the current. Try to keep the body horizontal to the water. This will reduce the danger of being pulled under. In fast, shallow rapids, lie on your back, feet pointing downstream, finning your hands alongside your hips. This action will increase buoyancy and help steer away from obstacles. Keep your feet up to avoid getting them caught by rocks.

In deep rapids, lie on your stomach, head downstream, and angling toward the shore. Watch for obstacles and be careful of backwater eddies and converging currents, as they often contain dangerous swirls.

Sudden immersion in cold water results in an immediate decline in skin temperature which, in turn, stimulates a cold-shock reflex. This reflex causes an instantaneous gasping for air and sudden increases in heart rate, respiratory rate, blood flow and blood pressure. The cold-shock reflex (see below for a more complete discussion) only lasts for a few minutes, but it can be deadly if the victim’s head is underwater (leading to immediate aspiration and drowning) or if the victim has no flotation assistance and cannot keep his/her head above the water.

A good rule to follow for accidental cold-water immersion (for example, falling though ice) is the “1-10-1” rule. In this concept, once a person falls into the water, he or she needs about 1 minute to get over the “cold shock” response and resume breathing normally. Most people die from drowning in this first minute, primarily caused by hyperventilation. They then have ~10 minutes to get out of the cold water before they experience skeletal muscle fatigue caused by low muscle temperatures. Finally, they have about an hour before moderate to severe hypothermia sets in.
There are many other flotation devices that can be devised by using some imagination. Just make sure to test the device before trying to use it.

conflict: Whether to enter moving water at all: FEMA P-2064 (2020, flood section) says 'Turn Around, Don't Drown' at flooded roadways, that 'Six inches of moving water may be enough to knock you off your feet', and to avoid wading in floodwater. ATP 3-50.21 (2018) gives techniques 'To ford a swift, treacherous stream' and to swim deep, swift rivers and rapids. The card puts the FEMA warning first and then the Army technique; the owner must decide how to present the two. Also, how long cold shock lasts: TB MED 508 (2026) says a person needs 'about 1 minute' to get over it; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) says it 'only lasts for a few minutes' (elsewhere 'the first 1-4 minutes'). The card shows both.

review.notes: Pass. Drafter flag verdicts: (a) FEMA 'six inches of moving water' vs Army fording: not a contradiction - FEMA addresses floodwater on roads, ATP 3-50.21 7-8 ff. addresses a deliberate stream crossing; leading with the FEMA warning, attributed and labelled 'at a flooded roadway', is the right order. (b) 'In deep rapids: lie on your stomach, head downstream, angling toward the shore' is ATP 3-50.21 7-12 almost word for word and sits right after the feet-first rule for fast shallow rapids (7-11), so the two positions are not confused; keep them adjacent as they are. All other lines faithful: plan from a high viewpoint, lowest water level, several channels/sandbar, start upstream, about 45 degrees, avoid rock ledges, estuaries, eddies, converging currents; pole 3 in by 7-8 ft planted upstream, foot below the pole, pole against the shoulder; group on one pole heaviest downstream; swim with the current, body horizontal; cold shock with TB MED 508's 1-10-1 rule and HHS 'a few minutes' both shown; test any flotation device. Kind protocol right. Optional: ATP 7-13 rope method for three or more people ('The length of the rope must be three times the width of the stream', figure 7-3) for the group ask. The kit has nothing on unbuckling a pack before crossing (searched).
